new_statements.quote: 7. Stress is almost invariably penultimate in Muna. This is also true for the other dialects and languages to be discussed. Stress is therefore not marked. [...] [p. 43-44, sec. 6 'Pancanic isolects':] Muna (J), Wolio (A), Cia-Cia (C), Kamaru (H), Lasalimu (E), Pancana (G) and Tukangbesi (B). [...] Obviously the closest relative of Muna is Pancana. The question is: what is Pancana? Which speech communities belong to it? Anceaux's Pancana (G) includes the following four isolects [...]: Palewata (10), Lawele (12), Kalende (20) and Lambusango (30), all located in central Buton. Bhurhanuddin's Pancana is made up of the following dialects: Kapontori, Kambowa, Kalende (subdialects Kalende and Lawele) and Labuandiri.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: File check: is present (32 pp., ScanSnap scan, no text layer; SIL archive copy), with the scanned (scanned/ etc.) and the page renders = printed p. 27) and = printed p. 44). I read both renders myself. p. 27, sec. 2 'Standard Muna phonology', point 7 reads exactly: "7. Stress is almost invariably penultimate in Muna. This is also true for the other dialects and languages to be discussed. Stress is therefore not marked." Points 5-6 on the same page (open V/CV syllables; two identical vowels = two syllables, la.a, ne.e) are as the reader describes. The second half of the composite quote (pp. 43-44, sec. 6 'Pancanic isolects') is verbatim on the p. 43 scanned and the p. 44 render, with the eli…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress falls on the penultimate syllable ('almost invariably'), stated for Standard Muna and extended by the author in one blanket sentence to all the other Muna dialects and Munic/Pancanic languages treated in the paper; Pancana (Anceaux's language G) is among the languages discussed, so stress is left unmarked in all cited forms. Because syllables are all open (V, CV) and identical vowel sequences count as two syllables (same page, points 5-6), penultimate syllable = penultimate vowel.
new_statements.exceptions: Only the hedge 'almost invariably'; no Pancana-specific exceptions. (For Muna proper, van den Berg 2003:100 notes siua 'nine' keeps antepenultimate stress after glide syllabification; that concerns Muna, not Pancana.)
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level statement based on wordlist (citation-form) data; a blanket remark in a comparative paper rather than a dedicated Pancana phonology. Crucially, van den Berg's own 1991 wordlists come from Busoa, Kambe-Kambero, Kaimbulawa/Lantoi, Liabuku, Kioko and Kambowa; none is from a Glottolog panc1247 dialect (Kapontori, Kalende, Labuandiri), so the statement applies to Pancana proper only by the author's extension. van den Berg 2003 (PL 550, p. 96), which does draw on his 'Pancana personal field notes', reconstructs 'Stress was penultimate' for Proto Muna-Buton without noting any modern exception.
new_statements.identity_note: The only stress statement is a blanket one: van den Berg (1991:27) describes Standard Muna and says penultimate stress 'is also true for the other dialects and languages to be discussed', and Pancana (Anceaux's language G) is discussed by name in sec. 6 (pp. 43-45). But his own wordlists there are from Busoa, Kambe-Kambero, Kaimbulawa, Liabuku (liab1237), Kioko (kiok1239) and Kambowa (counted as a Pancana dialect by Bhurhanuddin 1979 but moved by van den Berg to Kioko); none is from a Glottolog panc1247 dialect (Kapontori, Kalende, Labuandiri). So the statement reaches panc1247 proper only by extension across the 'Pancanic' group; treat it as a group-level, low-confidence entry. Note also that 'Pancana' is used locally as a broad ethnonym (Zamihu et al. 2024 blurb; Hidayatullah 2021 on Lakudo) covering Muna dialects on Buton (Gu-Lakudo, Mawasangka, Siompu) and Liabuku, whereas panc1247 is the Kapontori-Lawele-Labuandiri belt across central Buton. Local pronunciation per Donohue 2004 fn. 2 concerns the island name, not Pancana.

Stress is therefore not marked.' Pancana (Anceaux's language G; Bhurhanuddin's dialects Kapontori, Kambowa, Kalende, Labuandiri) is discussed by name in sec. 6 'Pancanic isolects' (pp. 43-45), but the author's own wordlists are from Busoa, Kambe-Kambero, Kaimbulawa, Liabuku, Kioko and Kambowa, none from a Glottolog panc1247 dialect. Verified visually on the page render.
